The abstraction of the social features of formally free labour and its exploitation is not Weber’s
aim, indeed quite the opposite. He needs this methodological device to highlight further specifics of
modern capitalism in comparison to that of antiquity. This comparison is conducted as an inventory of
differences. The characteristics of antiquity that had prevented its development toward modern
capitalism, were for Weber, first, the political specificity of the ancient political community (its social
structure, finance, tax farming, slavery, war) and, second, its economic uniqueness and singularity. He
outlines the latter as follows: production for the market was restricted in consequence of limits on the
transport capacity of goods from and into domestic territory. In addition, there was an economically
determined lability in capital stock and capital formation as well as the technical limitations of the
exploitation of slave labour in large enterprises.
Also, the possibility of rational calculation was restricted, especially because of the use of slave
labour. Added to this was the (politically and socially) precarious position of the entrepreneur in
ancient capitalism, which contrasts with those who used capital as a source of rent. The antichrematistic character of ancient political philosophy was another factor. Antiquity also lacked every
ethical transfiguration of gainful acquisition, which Weber had highlighted as a contribution of
Protestant ethics to the modern economic ethos.
These itemized economic characteristics are a mirror reflection of those of the modern capitalist
economy. The contrast of the two in terms of purely economic particularities is by itself insufficient.
Weber saw ancient capitalism essentially as a politically oriented capitalism, and here his
argumentation refers exclusively to the autonomous Greek polis and Rome, and not to other epochs of
antiquity, which were characterized by high economic intensity. The political orientation prevented
the highly developed capitalist economy of antiquity from moving in the direction of modern
entrepreneurial capitalism. The political and social structures did not direct the energies of citizens
into peaceful, rational acquisition through the market, as was the case for the citizenry of a defined
type of the autonomous medieval city. The highly developed capitalism of antiquity and modern
capitalism are distinguished, first, economically and, second, by their embedding in different political
structures, which in their turn partly determine those economic differences. Weber considered ancient
capitalism essentially to be a politically oriented capitalism. Weber’s analysis of the ancient economy,
which had a capitalist character, is not designed as a prehistory of capitalism. On the contrary, the
presentation emphasizes the differences and aims to refute the assumption that the ancient and modern
economies differ only in their dimensions. Weber was not interested in presenting a historical
development, but in analysing the development potential of a historical configuration, dependent not
only on economic, but above all on extra-economic factors.
This multifactorial analysis led to a result that was at odds with a widely accepted idea in economic
science at the time, namely that the development of the forms of the economy could be represented in
a progressive sequence of stages. Weber’s study of the ancient economy, on the other hand, showed
that the potential for development towards a capitalist economy was much higher at the time of the
Roman Republic than towards the end of the empire, whose economic form he tried to capture with
the concept of the oikos economy. The historical school (Rodbertus and his followers) had described

analysis of capitalism had to differentiate between different types of capitalism (ancient and modern
capitalism, politically or economically oriented capitalism, rentier capitalism, commercial capitalism).

[…] For the burghers of the [medieval] city, military strength could serve as a support, but
in inland areas it could not serve as the basis of their economic acquisition. By the fact that
the seat of the highest military force was not in the cities, the acquisitive interest of the
burghers of the city depended on the development of rational economic means
(ibid.: 289; Weber 1962: 238–9).
In contrast, the demos of the ancient polis, with its chronic wars
over land and human property, “such a demos could not possibly be oriented primarily in the direction
of pacific economic acquisition and rational economic enterprise” (ibid.: 288; Weber 1962: 237). The
Periclean ruling position – fifth-century Athens is the model here – was based on the interests of the
corporation of the citizens, those with full rights, in the political expansion of the city, while the
ancient freedmen, like the city inhabitants of the Hellenistic and imperial non-autonomous city later
on, were a stratum of peaceful acquisitive people – Homines oeconomici – who were close to the
acquisitive bourgeoisie of the Middle Ages and modern times (ibid.: 281). The thrust of the unfinished
text is clear. It is about the analysis of the factors that contributed to the development of modern
rational economic behaviour and rational economic instruments in a certain political-economic type of
city. Formulated in terms of social history, it is about the emergence of the modern acquisitive
bourgeoisie, as Weber then phrases it in 1920 both in his lectures on economic and social history and
in the Vorbemerkung (Prefatory Remarks to the Collected Essays in the Sociology of Religion; Weber
2004b) as well as in other places.

4.5

OCCIDENT AND ORIENT

In the introductory chapter of Die Stadt (MWG I22–5), Weber had already sketched the beginning of
a comparison between medieval European cities and Oriental cities. The text breaks off, however,

without this comparison being completed. However, he takes it up again from the perspective of the
problem of the emergence of modern capitalism, in his Wirtschaftsethik der Weltreligionen,
successively published between 1915 and 1918 in the Archive, and then republished in an expanded
version in 1920 and 1921. We will limit ourselves here to brief remarks on China. Weber’s
examination of the economic ethics of Confucianism begins with a detailed analysis of the
Sociological Foundations: A. City, Prince and God; B. Feudal and Prebendal State; C. Administration
and Agrarian Constitution; D. Self-government, Law and Capitalism. Here, as in the following
chapters on the Literatenstand (The Literati), Confucian orientation to life and Taoism, the focus is on
the factors and conditions that had inhibited or prevented the development of the Chinese economy in
the direction of modern corporate capitalism. Just a few remarks on Weber’s analysis of the Chinese
city.
In Konfuzianismus (Confucianism; MWG I/19; Weber 1951), Weber operates with a juxtaposition
of two ideally constructed city types: City of the Orient versus City of the Occident. The construction
of this opposition goes back to his essay Die Stadt mentioned above. In this essay, the chapter Die
Stadt des Okzidents (The City of the Occident) begins with the following sentence: “The Medieval
occidental city presents striking contrasts to its Asiatic counterparts. This was particularly true for
urban formations norths of the Alps where the Western city developed in its purest form” (Weber 1962
: 97; MWG I/22–5: 100).
For Weber, the construction of an ideal type is always the function of a precise research question.
If the question changes, then the construction of the ideal-type, which is not the goal but the
instrument of research, also changes. The comparison of the ideal-typical ancient and medieval
autonomous city was based on the question of the specific nature of the profit opportunities that
determined urban economic policy. The comparison of the ideal-typical autonomous medieval city
south and north of the Alps was determined by the same question and came to the conclusion that in
the south it was political, and in the north, it was economic opportunities for profit. The ideal-typical
comparison between the occidental and oriental city pursued the question of how the lack of urban
autonomy, of a bourgeoisie and of an urban economic policy shaped economic development in China.
Weber describes China as a country of cities and huge internal trade. However, given the
overriding importance of agricultural production, the monetary economy was relatively weakly
developed.17 Only trade with Europe and the resulting increase in the influx of precious metals from
the Mexican and Peruvian silver mines brought about a significant change here. He now states that the
strengthening of the money economy, especially in finance, did not bring about any capitalist
phenomena, but, on the contrary, increased traditionalism. Nor had the colossal increase in the
population provided any incentive for a “capitalist shaping of the economy”, but was linked to “(at
least!) a stationary form of the economy” (MWS I/19: 36–7). Strong population growth, circulation of
precious metals and strengthening of the money economy, were factors that in economic history at the
time of Weber were seen as decisive for the modernization of the economy and the emergence of
capitalism.
Weber observes a contrary development for China and seeks an explanation for it. The starting
point of his search for an explanation is the observation, “In the Occident, in antiquity and in the
Middle Ages, the cities, and in the Middle Ages, the curia and the emerging state were the bearers of
financial rationalization, the money economy and politically oriented capitalism” (MWS I/19: 37).
There was nothing corresponding to this in China. We can only briefly mention one point from Weber’
s long discussion on the Chinese economy and social order, his comparison of the occidental and
oriental city regarding capitalism.

Of course, Chinese cities had much in common with ancient or medieval occidental cities. They
could be fortresses or residences of princes and high officials. Economically, the major consumers
spent annuity income (land rents, official sinecures and other politically conditioned income). As
everywhere else, the cities were the seat of merchants and, although much less exclusive than in the
Occident, the seat of Gewerbe. Nor did the cities have a state-guaranteed market monopoly, market
rights also existed in the villages. According to Weber, however, something else was decisive. “The
basic antithesis of Chinese, as of all Oriental city formation, however, was the absence of the special
political character of the city” (MWS I/19: 37).
This is followed by the inventory of differences typical of Weber’s method, which cannot be
reproduced here in detail, i.e. everything that the Chinese city was not in comparison to the occidental
one: not a “polis” in the ancient sense – it had no city law – it did not know a city bourgeoisie like the
ancient world, in the sense of a city-based military class, nor a city bourgeoisie like the Middle Ages –
no city freedom – it did not form a community. Although there were a variety of professional
associations such as guilds or guilds that “held the regulation of the economic life of the city in their
hands”, they had “much less legally guaranteed ‘self-government’ than the villages” (ibid.: 38). The
city, as a rational product of the imperial administration, could not carry out a “city economic policy”;
it lacked the “legal foundations of a free, cooperatively regulated constitution of industry and
commerce” (ibid.: 42).

4.6

ATTEMPT AT A BALANCE SHEET

Under the heading “Historical Studies”, we have placed three very different texts by Weber in a
context. Two ideas in particular construct this context. One is the above-mentioned definition of the
field of economics formulated in 1904, as Weber and Sombart claimed it to be. Another idea is that
these three studies on antiquity, the Middle Ages and Chinese history are direct continuations of the
investigations into the emergence of modern capitalism that Weber had initiated with Die
protestantische Ethik. In summary, the following can be said.
In the 1909 version of Agrarverhältnisse im Altertum (MWG I/6; Weber 1976a), Max Weber
examines the agrarian history of antiquity from the perspective of urban (political-social) organization
regarding urban economic systems. In retrospect, but only very shortly later, in 1910, Weber specifies
in his Antikritisches Schlußwort zum ‘Geist des Kapitalismus’ (Weber 2001) that he had formed in the
Agrarverhältnisse for the capitalism of antiquity as an economic system an ideal-typical mental
picture of the specifically different features in contrast to other epochs. This comparison is made on
the basis of a long series of criteria. Regarding our topic, Weber’s analysis of the obstacles to the
development of capitalism in antiquity only mentions the factor that he places in first place, the
political character of the ancient communities. This peculiarity also included the “abundance of class
differentiations of the population and political differentiations of property (especially land and
inheritance) law, which could and did become sources of income of all kinds, especially of rents”
(MWG I/6: 357–9).
Weber then comes to the following overall conclusion: Firstly, the development of the ancient
economy and ancient capitalism does not proceed with a tendency towards convergence, but on the
contrary with a tendency towards distance from the structural features of modern capitalism ( ibid.:
713–4). Secondly, the epoch in antiquity in which capitalism reaches its height is at the same time
when the type of rationality of urban economic policy differs radically from that of medieval urban

economic policy, which in turn forms the starting point of the development towards modern
capitalism. According to Weber, the reverse was true in Hellenism and the Roman Empire. Here, the
development of Gewerbe (industry; ibid.: 725) and the economic rationality of the economic policy (if
one can still speak of such) of the cities correspond to those of the medieval cities. Both, however,
coincide with the decline of ancient capitalism, whereas “medieval urban development was by no
means the sole decisive precursor for [modern capitalism and the modern state], and was not at all its
carrier, but it is nevertheless indispensable as a highly decisive factor in their emergence” (MWG I/22–
5: 233).
In his posthumously published study Die Stadt, Weber analyses the urban economic policy of
antiquity and the Middle Ages as a policy of Verbände (associations). The medieval city appears as an
economically regulating association, the ancient city, in ideal-typical exaggeration, as an economic
association. The political-legal structure of the autonomous ancient and autonomous medieval city has
the quality of “an association of ‘citizens’, socialized in the form of an institution, equipped with
special and characteristic organs, which in this quality of theirs are subject to a common law
accessible only to them, i.e., are corporative legal associates” (ibid.: 107). It is certainly no
coincidence that in Die Stadt Weber concludes his analysis of urban economic policy as associational
action in the ideal-typical comparison of Homo politicus (ancient city, composed of citizens’ guild and
warriors’ guild, the economic action of which is primarily politically and militarily oriented) and
Homo œconomicus (medieval city being primarily economically oriented), thus taking up a central
category of contemporary economic neo-classicism. However, he uses it in a completely different way
when he writes: “The political situation of the medieval urban citizen pointed him on the way to being
homo œconomicus” (ibid: 275). For Weber, it is not the nature of man that makes him Homo
œconomicus. On the contrary, the cause is certain structural conditions – political, military,
geographical, etc. – of the association to which the economically active person belongs. In the case of
the medieval burgher, it was these structural conditions that pointed him “towards the path of rational
economic means” (ibid.: 289). In decisive contrast to the city bourgeois of the Middle Ages as well as
to the stratum of freedmen it “pointed to the path of a relatively modern bourgeois acquisition” within
the framework of Rome’s politically oriented capitalism, the “typical demos of the full bourgeois in
the Hellenic city, monopolizing the politically conditioned rents: state rents, daily allowances,
mortgage rents, land rents”, “could not possibly be primarily oriented in the direction of pacified
economic acquisition and a rational economic enterprise” (ibid.: 282–3, 288).
In a next step, Weber contrasts the generally comparable structure of the legal order, but different
economic order, in the ancient and medieval city with the relationship between legal and economic
order in the Chinese city. As a basic contrast between the Chinese and the occidental city, Weber
insists in Confucianism on the absence of the special political character of the city in the Orient. It was
not a polis, it knew no city law, it was not a commune with special political rights. There was also a
complete absence of the political oath of allegiance of the city’s inhabitants. The regulation of
economic life was largely in the hands of various associations of the city’s inhabitants. The city itself
was not a Verband (status organization) and had no legal personality. There was no city economic
policy, no system of guild privileges, no reliable legal basis for a free, cooperatively regulated
constitution of industry and trade (MWG I/19: 158). There was no legal codification in land tenure
law. The only way out was to preserve the clan as a self-help association ( ibid.: 249–50). The legal
forms and sociological foundations of the capitalist enterprise were lacking (ibid.: 257–8). Those
“organisational structures of an economic nature which went beyond the framework of the individual
economy in general” rested on real or imitated personal kinship (ibid.: 273). According to Weber, the

patrimonial character of administration and law-making stood in the way of a rationally calculable
functioning of administration and administration of justice, which was needed by a trade that was
developing into a rational business (ibid.: 279). Ethically oriented patrimonialism and the edicts of the
emperor produced codifications of ethical, non-legal norms; justice remained Kadi justice (ibid.: 281–
2).
What Weber analyses in these studies, cited here as examples and only in a very abbreviated way,
are relations between economic orders and legal orders. However, this is not what he is concerned
with, at least not in such a non-specific way. His question is, on the one hand, about the nature of
urban economic policy and the factors that determine it, and, on the other hand, about the impact of a
certain type of urban economic policy (as a policy of association) on the creation of forms of
enterprise, legal forms and legal guarantees that could foster the emergence of modern rational
enterprise capitalism. In China, the absence of urban associations as bearers of the law, as regulatory
bodies of the economy and as bearers of urban economic policy were among the specifically different
features of a patrimonially constituted economic, legal and political order, whose economic
development differed decisively from the occidental one in this respect, among others. In his last
lecture, in Munich in 1919–2018 after the end of the war (see Whimster in this volume), and in the
famous Vorbemerkung (Prefatory Remarks) of 1920 to the Gesammelte Aufsätze zur
Religionssoziologie (Collected Essays in the Sociology of Religion; Weber 2004b), Weber’s central
point of view becomes clear once again. In his lecture on universal economic and social history,
Weber takes up the results of his urban studies under the title: IV. The Emergence of Modern
Capitalism, §7 The bourgeoisie. In the Vorbemerkung, which can be read as a kind of retrospective
formulation of his research programme, Max Weber takes stock of the fact that:
in a universal history of culture the central problem for us is not in the last analysis, even
from a purely economic view-point the development of capitalist activity as such, differing
in different cultures only in form: the adventure type, or capitalism in trade, war, politics, or
administration as sources of gain. It is rather the origin of this bourgeois business capitalism
with its rational organization of free labour. Or, in terms of cultural history, the problem is
that of the origin of the Western bourgeois class and of its distinctiveness, a problem which
is certainly closely connected with that of the origin of the capitalistic organization of
labour, but is not quite the same thing.
(Weber 2004b: 107–108)
In the words he employed at the same time in his unfinished sociology, the problem of his historical
studies was the “connections of economic dynamics with the social order” (MWG I/23: 151). In order
to be able to uncover these connections under the question of the emergence of the modern state and
modern capitalism, just as detailed historical, empirical investigations were needed as those produced
by the historical school. Now, however, for Weber and Sombart, historical investigation in economics
has to be theory-led, i.e., by “rational construction of concepts, types and systems” (Sombart & Weber
2012: 302).19

Perspectives micro et macro
sur l’économie antique :
à propos de deux publications
récentes sur Polanyi, Weber et Finley
HINNERK BRUHNS

A

UJOURD’HUI, LA RÉFLEXION SUR LA NATURE DE L’ÉCONOMIE des époques pré-modernes est
alimentée, d’un côté, par l’enrichissement de la documentation historique et archéologique, de
l’autre, par la relecture critique de certains textes « fondateurs » du XXe siècle. Des deux ouvrages
traités dans la note critique qui suit, le premier réunit les deux perspectives, sans toutefois viser
un équilibre, le second se place résolument dans la seconde et tente d’atteindre, à partir du débat
sur l’économie antique, une vision macro-historique sur la singularité de la démocratie athénienne.

Autour de Polanyi. Vocabulaires, théories et modalités des échanges. Nanterre, 12-14 juin 2004.
Textes réunis par Ph. CLANCIER, F. JOANNÈS, P. ROUILLARD et A. TENU (Colloques de la Maison
René-Ginouvès, sous la direction de Pierre Rouillard, vol. I), Paris, De Boccard, 2005, XI, 290 p.
Ce livre réunit vingt contributions, réparties en deux parties et cinq sections (I. Les débats :
modernité, relecture ; II. De l’Orient ancien aux Aztèques : Orient ancien, monde Grec, Amériques),
suivies d’une riche conclusion de Natalie Zemon Davis. À un moment où la publication d’Actes
de Colloque est décriée, il faut saluer cette entreprise qui va à contre-courant, permettant au
lecteur de découvrir, comme s’il avait assisté au Colloque, la diversité des points de vue sur l’apport de Polanyi à la connaissance des économies des sociétés anciennes, précapitalistes, et la pertinence, ou non, des catégories centrales de redistribution, réciprocité et échange. Certes, le lecteur
aurait souhaité trouver également un écho des débats qui ont eu lieu lors du Colloque, que l’on
imagine vifs, mais, mise à part la juxtaposition brute de certaines positions divergentes, voire
opposées, seule la conclusion en donne quelques reflets.
Le parcours de Polanyi et l’apparition des concepts-clefs sont traités par Karl Polanyi Levitt
et Anne Chapman dans des chapitres introductifs fort utiles. Contrairement aux lectures habituelles, Karl Polanyi met au centre de l’œuvre de son père la notion d’économie désencastrée.
Anne Chapman, par contre, part des notions de « embedded economy », « substantive meaning
of economy », en s’opposant à la vision des « formal economists ». Jérôme Maucourant (« Le troc

 

[PDF p. 3]
Anabases 7

5/03/08 15:50

Page 224

HINNERK BRUHNS

et la monnaie dans la pensée de Polanyi ») s’interroge sur les fondements de l’économie 1. En
affirmant qu’il n’y a pas de « nature » de l’homme le vouant au troc, Polanyi avait invalidé le
postulat de la vieille économie politique anglaise. Prenant appui sur la démonstration de Polanyi,
Maucourant dénonce la théorie actuelle de la « monnaie souveraine » comme une tendance excessive à essentialiser le fait monétaire et à produire un mythe symétrique à la fable du troc. Le
thème de la société et de l’économie sans marché, thème central du livre, est introduit par
J. Renger. Ce qui apparaissait à Polanyi comme l’évolution d’une société caractérisée par des
« reciprocal economic structures » vers une société à caractère redistributif, est pour Renger, sur
la base de nouvelles sources, mais aussi d’une relecture de la documentation utilisée par Polanyi,
un système dans lequel les deux formes d’économie coexistaient et interagissaient.
La deuxième section (« Relecture ») s’ouvre par une « Critique de la trilogie réciprocité,
redistribution, échange » dans laquelle Alain Testart prend le contre-pied des positions défendues
depuis longtemps par Renger et d’autres partisans de Polanyi. Très rares seraient, dans l’histoire,
les cas connus de systèmes de redistributions (comme l’évergétisme étudié par Paul Veyne). Les
royautés archaïques ne seraient pas caractérisées par la redistribution, ni au sens de l’économie
politique, ni au sens des Polanyiens, c’est-à-dire à partir d’un centre, dans les principaux secteurs
de l’économie. Et ce concept, trop marqué au goût de Testart par l’idée de don et contre-don,
néglige selon lui toute la dimension de l’extorsion dans les relations « économiques ». Si Polanyi
est fréquemment lu comme un critique de la société de marché, Jean-Michel Servet apporte un
point de vue d’économiste et s’emploie à montrer que cette lecture mène en erreur et, qu’au
contraire, il faut dépasser l’opposition habituelle entre don et marché. La notion même de
marché prendrait un sens différent si l’on s’appuyait sur l’opposition des logiques de place de
marché et de lien de clientèle. L’économie de marché telle qu’elle est présentée dans nombre d’interprétations de la pensée de Polanyi n’existe pas, et quant à la soi-disant extension de la « sphère
marchande », nous sommes victimes d’une illusion d’optique, puisqu’en fait nous assistons à un
déplacement de la limite morale des échanges. La mise en cause de la doctrine de l’altérité fondamentale de l’économie antique est poursuivie par Alain Bresson qui critique de façon substantielle les concepts d’économie encastrée et d’économie substantive vs formelle (ainsi que leur
application schématique aux sociétés anciennes), et la séparation artificielle des logiques institutionnelle et économique. Car la société capitaliste relève de la même logique d’analyse que les
sociétés pré-capitalistes. La démonstration de Bresson est bien argumentée, mais elle aurait été
encore plus convaincante si l’auteur n’avait pas mis Max Weber avec Polanyi dans le même sac
du primitivisme. Faut-il rappeler les pages de Weber sur le capitalisme antique ? La critique
méthodologique du concept polanyien d’économie substantive aurait pu s’appuyer avantageusement sur la distinction fondamentale, établie par Weber, entre Haushalten (l’utilisation et l’acquisition continues [par la production et l’échange] de biens pour assurer (a) son
approvisionnement ou (b) l’obtention d’autres biens qui seront utilisés pour son propre usage) et
Erwerben (un comportement guidé par les chances de gain, c’est-à-dire les chances d’acquérir
[une fois ou de façon régulière] de nouveaux droits pour disposer de biens ; Économie et société,
chap. II, §10 et §11). Car, pour Weber, la même logique d’analyse s’applique aux sociétés
anciennes et modernes, et il s’agit de déterminer, dans chaque système économique particulier,

Voir également le beau livre de J. MAUCOURANT, Avez-vous lu Polanyi ?, Paris, La
Dispute/SNÉDIT, 2005.

les éléments qui relèvent de l’économie substantive ou formelle (pour parler comme Polanyi), ou
des deux types différents d’activité économique que sont Haushalten et Erwerben.
La section « Orient ancien » est composée de six contributions. Bertrand Lafont s’interroge
sur la persistance de l’opposition, apparemment irréductible en assyriologie, entre Polanyiens et
Anti-Polanyiens qui, tous deux, travaillent à partir des mêmes sources. L’auteur voit l’explication
dans la nature souvent ambiguë des informations fournies par la documentation, ainsi que dans
des approches marquées par des présupposés idéologiques ou méthodologiques. Le problème
serait donc au fond, pourrait-on ajouter, que l’on ne fait pas toujours le meilleur usage de
Polanyi. Cécile Michel reprend les thèses de Polanyi concernant la nature du commerce des
Assyriens sur la base d’une documentation et d’études largement renouvelées, mettant l’accent
sur le caractère privé et familial de l’organisation du commerce. Un correctif différent est apporté
par Marcello Rede qui montre la nécessité d’intégrer des éléments du contexte politique dans
l’analyse économique. Le binôme central/local s’avère ainsi plus pertinent que celui de
public/privé pour l’analyse du cas de Larsa. De même, le concept de « commerce administré » se
comprend mieux à partir de la situation politique, en l’occurrence la domination babylonienne,
qui imprimait à certains segments du commerce de Larsa un caractère d’exploitation politique.
Plusieurs contributions étudient en détail la possibilité d’utiliser des concepts polanyiens
pour la compréhension des situations et pratiques économiques reflétées par des dossiers de
sources spécifiques. Catherine Sauvage tente d’appliquer (avec prudence) l’opposition polanyienne entre facteur et mercator aux commerçants d’Ougarit (attributions royales combinées
avec des activités « privées » parallèles) et à ceux d’Égypte, où il n’y avait pas de commerçants à
proprement parler (commerce international entre les mains de grands fonctionnaires et de
personnes proches du pouvoir royal). Le concept d’économie d’oikos est abordé par Michael Jursa
à propos des « temple households » à Babylone. Ce concept semble inapproprié pour différentes
raisons : le temple dépend de travailleurs loués à l’extérieur ; on observe une monétarisation croissante, y compris pour les salaires ; la demande d’argent croissante entraîne une concentration sur
des cultures de rapport (cash crops), destinées au marché et, dans sa suite, un certain degré de
spécialisation économique.
Partant, à l’instar de Catherine Sauvage, de la typologie polanyienne facteur / mercator,
Laetitia Graslin-Thomé et Christel Vivel proposent d’utiliser la typologie beaucoup plus différenciée des activités de l’entrepreneur, élaborée, dans le sillage de Schumpeter et de la tradition
autrichienne, par Lachmann : activités de marchand, de direction, de gestion du capital, fonction entrepreneuriale, etc., et de poser aux sources historiques les questions du risque, de l’innovation, et ainsi de suite. Regarder l’économie de l’Orient ancien avec les yeux de l’école
autrichienne de l’économie est certes stimulant, mais l’analyse fine des types d’activités du
commerçant antique (ou la « dé-composition » de l’activité de l’entrepreneur en ses multiples
facettes) et sa mise en parallèle virtuelle avec les commerçants du XXe siècle reste insatisfaisante
tant que les facettes ainsi isolées ne sont pas considérés comme appartenant à (ou étant déterminées par) un système économique dont la connaissance serait l’objectif principal.
On passe ensuite au monde grec, d’abord avec une étude de Catherine Perlès sur les
échanges dans le Néolithique, puis avec une contribution d’Evelyne Scheid-Tissinier sur « Le
Monde d’Ulysse » de Moses I. Finley qui avait lui-même rappelé ses dettes envers Polanyi.
L’accent est mis sur le comportement des aristocrates engagés dans des pratiques de don et de
contre-don, mais qui, à l’occasion, passaient à des activités « commerciales » (vente de prisonniers
de guerre, etc.). Avec Nicola Parise, on revient à un plaidoyer « pro Polanyi » dont l’approche

 

[PDF p. 5]
Anabases 7

5/03/08 15:50

Page 226

HINNERK BRUHNS

« substantive » permettrait de mieux rendre compte de l’autonomie des deux modes de circulation (métal / monnaie). Sans parler de Polanyi, Raymond Descat aborde une question centrale
dans la problématique générale de Polanyi. La naissance du marché en Grèce, un marché régulé
et régulateur, contrôlé par la Cité, représente une évolution liée à la suppression de la servitude
pour dettes, d’une part, à la transformation du statut des esclaves « importés » de l’extérieur et
considérés comme des « biens », de l’autre. La question du marché revient dans la relecture
d’Aristote par Christophe Pébarthe : Aristote ne découvre pas l’économie (comme l’avait affirmé
le titre d’un fameux article de Polanyi) : il combat le marché.
Après ce parcours à travers l’Orient ancien et la Grèce, deux études sur l’économie des
Maya (Pierre Becquelin) et des Aztèques (Anne Chapman) s’appuient à la fois sur des données
archéologiques et des sources espagnoles du temps de la conquête. Système de redistribution sans
marché, contrôlé par les prêtres, d’un côté, système de redistribution avec un puissant marché,
contrôlé par le palais, de l’autre côté : l’utilisation des concepts polanyiens à des fins heuristiques
aboutit ici, comme dans d’autres études rassemblées dans ce livre, à un résultat ambigu. Que l’on
puisse identifier « réciprocité, redistribution, échange sans véritable économie de marché, et
présence du troc » et donc « coexistence de différents mécanismes dans un même système »
(p. 266) n’est pas une véritable surprise. La question est de savoir comment on peut passer,
malgré les lacunes de nos documentations, d’une description d’éléments partiels ou de « différents mécanismes » à une compréhension des systèmes économiques précapitalistes. Système économique pris dans le sens que lui avait donné l’inventeur de ce concept, Werner Sombart (Le
capitalisme moderne, 1902).
Mohammad NAFISSI, Ancient Athens & Modern Ideology. Value, Theory & Evidence in
Historical Sciences : Max Weber, Karl Polanyi & Moses Finley (Bulletin of the Institute of Classical
Studies Supplement 80.), xii + 325 p., Londres, Institute of Classical Studies, School of
Advanced Study, University of London, 2005, ISBN : 0-900587-91-1, £50.
Un titre prometteur et suggestif : avec une étude sur Weber, Polanyi et Finley, l’on
comprend que l’auteur se propose de revisiter les grands débats du XXe siècle sur l’économie
antique et qu’il se placera au niveau de la théorie et de la conceptualisation. Un livre bien fait :
une structure limpide, un index utile, une thèse clairement énoncée et défendue, une démarche
bien expliquée. Et pourtant, pour dire les choses d’emblée : un livre qui ne convainc pas, aussi
stimulant soit-il en certains endroits, un livre qui irrite même.
Le point de départ est original, car c’est avec les yeux d’un descendant des vaincus de la
bataille de Marathon que l’auteur, originaire d’Iran, s’est mis à étudier la Grèce antique et à s’intéresser au « paradoxe de Marx ». C’est-à-dire à la question de savoir comment une civilisation
basée sur une économie esclavagiste, « primitive », a pu atteindre les sommets de la culture,
comment la démocratie athénienne a pu vaincre la Perse, et quelles étaient, finalement, les
chances d’existence d’une démocratie sans capitalisme. Considérant la démocratie directe des
Athéniens comme un défi (il parle même de « menace » : threat, p. 2) à la fois pour la monarchie
patrimoniale des Perses et pour la démocratie des Anglo-Saxons, l’entrée en la matière lui était
tout naturellement l’œuvre de Moses I. Finley. Mais comment lire Finley sans revenir à Max
Weber ? Et comment revenir de Weber à Finley sans passer par Karl Polanyi ? La trame du livre
se dessinait ainsi tout naturellement.

PERSPECTIVES MICRO ET MACRO SUR L’ÉCONOMIE ANTIQUE

Seulement, en choisissant comme axe central de l’analyse et de la comparaison des trois
auteurs la querelle entre primitivistes et modernistes, et en limitant ses points de vue à l’alternative « pour/contre/médiation », Nafissi ne semble pas avoir été conscient du risque qu’il prenait.
Traiter de la lecture contestable (tout au moins en partie) que Finley a faite de Weber, sans
prendre connaissance des travaux existants sur la question (et même en anglais !), a pour conséquence que Nafissi enfonce des portes ouvertes. Traiter de l’économie antique dans l’œuvre de
Weber, et notamment dans la perspective du conflit entre modernistes et primitivistes, sans
connaître les nombreux travaux italiens, allemands et français, publiés sur ce sujet au cours des
vingt dernières années, ne peut qu’irriter le lecteur averti et mettre sur de fausses pistes les lecteurs
non spécialistes, en premier lieu les étudiants, mais aussi les lecteurs venant d’autres champs des
sciences sociales 2. Ignorer superbement les travaux publiés en d’autres langues que l’anglais
devient, certes, une habitude de plus en plus répandue, mais cela ne lui confère pas pour autant
une once de légitimité 3.
C’est dommage et regrettable, car parmi ces trois cents pages, nombreuses sont celles qui
valent la peine d’être lues. Par exemple, celles qui sont consacrées aux rapports entre l’école historique allemande de l’économie, d’une part, Carl Menger et l’école autrichienne de l’autre. On lira
avec profit la bonne analyse des tensions entre Eduard Meyer et Karl Bücher, déclenchées par la
réaction violente de Meyer à la parution de Die Entstehung der Volkswirtschaft (1893) de Bücher.
Cependant, en ce qui concerne la position de Weber par rapport à ce conflit, Nafissi en reste aux
lectures habituelles. Il aurait fallu étudier la correspondance de Weber, et surtout Économie et
société, pour comprendre en quoi résidait l’importance de Bücher pour Weber 4. Dans le chapitre
introductif aux Agrarverhältnisse im Altertum (1909), intitulé « Zur ökonomischen Theorie der
antiken Staatenwelt », Weber avait pris la défense de Bücher, expliquant que les Wirtschaftsstufen
devaient être comprises comme des Idealtypen, ce que Bücher lui-même n’avait pas compris –
comme le montrera sa contribution au premier volume du Grundriss der Sozialökonomie en 1914.
Affirmer donc, comme le fait Nafissi – et il en fait même sa thèse principale –que, pour Weber,
l’Antiquité se situe au niveau du stade économique de l’oikos et compter Weber, malgré quelques
ouvertures envers les « modernistes », dans le bataillon des primitivistes est tout simplement un
malentendu.
Cette position de départ erronée fausse dès lors toute l’argumentation du livre.
Contrairement à ce qu’affirme l’auteur dans le chapitre 4, l’objectif central de Weber n’était pas
« to settle the oikos controversy ». Cette controverse n’avait qu’une importance tout à fait secondaire par rapport à la problématique de recherche de Weber dans ses Agrarverhältnisse, à savoir
comprendre le système du capitalisme antique et ses différences par rapport au système écono2
3

4

Le dossier publié par trois éminents sociologues dans Contemporary Sociology, organe de
l’American Sociological Association, 36/5, septembre 2007, en est une bonne illustration.
Certains titres allemands sont cités dans la bibliographie, notamment les textes fondateurs
des années 1900, mais il ne s’agit que de citations. Aucun titre français ou italien n’y apparaît.
Cf. P. SPAHN, « Max Weber et la typologie des modes d’activités industrielles de Karl
Bücher », in H. BRUHNS & J. ANDREAU (éd.), Sociologie économique et économie de
l’Antiquité : à propos de Max Weber (Cahiers du Centre de recherches historiques, 34,
octobre 2004), p. 115-132.

 

[PDF p. 7]

HINNERK BRUHNS

mique du capitalisme moderne. La tentative de Nafissi de « rendre sa vraie place » à ce grand texte
de Weber se solde ainsi par un échec prévisible, et la discussion de l’auteur sur Athènes et
Mycènes retombe dans un évolutionnisme dépassé.
Les longues pages sur la méthodologie de Weber n’apportent rien de nouveau ; pour l’essentiel, il s’agit là d’un débat, interne au Royaume-Uni, avec Sam Whimster. Et quant à la
méthode idéaltypique, l’auteur témoigne des mêmes difficultés de compréhension que Finley luimême. La fameuse construction idéaltypique de la cité antique, opposée à la ville médiévale (dans
Die Stadt 5), est curieusement absente du livre de Nafissi, à part une allusion absolument incompréhensible à l’« idealized picture of the ancient polis » de Weber (p. 287) 6. On en reste ainsi au
stade d’une lecture idéologique et d’une mécompréhension regrettable de la méthodologie de
Weber. Quand Nafissi écrit « I hope to have shown that AG [= Agrarverhältnisse im Altertum]
simply represents Weber’s first and perhaps most coherent attempt to realize the project that
emerges from his methodological writings of 1903-06 » et qu’un des objectifs de Weber était « to
strike a middle course between the modernist historians and primitivist political economists »
(p. 119), il ne reproduit malheureusement que des lectures anciennes, superficielles, qui ignorent
le véritable objectif de Weber, lié à la fois au travaux de Werner Sombart et à sa propre étude du
capitalisme moderne : l’analyse d’un système économique pré-moderne.
La partie du livre consacrée à Polanyi est plus solide, et elle présente l’avantage de s’appuyer
en partie sur des documents d’archives non publiés. Nafissi s’intéresse aux liens entre Polanyi et
Finley, ainsi que, par la suite, aux revirements de Finley par rapport à Polanyi. La présentation
du parcours intellectuel et politique de Finley est riche en détails et nourrie d’une bonne connaissance de son œuvre. Les chapitres consacrés à l’historien de Cambridge débouchent sur le constat
de l’incohérence du Finley des dernières années : « The uneasy cohabitation of economic primitivism and political modernism » (p. 277). Un constat analogue avait été fait à propos de « l’obsession de Weber pour la question de la rationalité bureaucratique comme caractéristique du
monde moderne », obsession qui aurait limité « his interest in and use of classical antiquity as un
attainable and hence politically useless model, except for the purpose of reinforcing the dark side
of his Janus-faced view of bureaucracy. » (p. 122). C’est joliment dit, mais cela n’a rien à voir avec
l’intérêt de Max Weber pour l’Antiquité.
Selon Nafissi, c’est grâce à ses compétences d’antiquisant professionnel que Moses Finley a
pu dépasser à la fois Weber et Polanyi (sans oublier Marx) dans la compréhension de l’économie
et de la démocratie grecques. Comment Nafissi compte-t-il aller maintenant plus loin que
Finley ? Il développe son argumentation autour du concept de « disembedded economy » :
Athènes est à la fois le lieu de naissance de la modernité politique et de la modernité économique ; à l’invention du politique correspond l’invention de l’économie (p. 269). L’économie
grecque n’était pas, comme on l’a répété après Polanyi, une économie encastrée mais tout au
contraire une « disembedded economy », et les Grecs étaient « better laissez-fairists than the
moderns have ever been » (p. 186). Le « désencastrement » économique suivait un double mouve5

ment : par rapport au politique, d’une part, et, d’autre part, à l’intérieur de l’économie, par la
rationalisation et la différenciation croissantes des activités (p. 261). Nafissi propose de repenser
le rapport entre esclaves et citoyens, riches et pauvres, luttes des classes et conflits, de refuser, à
propos des esclaves, l’alternative entre classes et groupes de statut et de comprendre que l’État
athénien avait un « quasi social-democratic character » (p. 260).
Mettre en question l’idée de l’encastrement et affirmer le contraire pourrait être une
démarche utile, s’il s’agissait d’une provocation contrôlée et si l’auteur ne se laissait pas trop facilement emporter par la tentation de raisonner par analogies, et de nous proposer ainsi tout
simplement une lecture libérale et social-démocrate de la société et de l’économie athéniennes.
Repenser le rapport entre le politique et l’économique ? Oui, certes. Mais le concept d’économie
désencastrée, appliqué à Athènes, est-il vraiment moins nébuleux et plus opérationnel que celui
d’économie encastrée ? En fin de compte, ne faudrait-il pas combiner autrement la relecture de
nos classiques avec les recherches récentes (archéologiques, historiques et anthropologiques) sur
le marché, et plus généralement sur l’économie en Grèce ancienne, comme dans d’autres sociétés pré-modernes ?

Max Weber’s ‘Basic Concepts’ in the Context
of his Studies in Economic History1
Hinnerk Bruhns

It would be a relatively easy, if time-consuming, task to assess the
importance of economic history for Max Weber by reviewing his writings from 1889 to 1920 and in this way establishing that economic
history was for him ubiquitous and dominant. One could go further,
and emphasise that problems of an economic-historical nature make
up a large part of his scholarly problematic. Weber had stated as much
when addressing his Munich students, expressed as an idiomatic critique of the materialist conception of history:
In conclusion, it should be emphasised that economic history (including

Debate over the Nature and Method of Economics

of ‘concept’ and ‘type’ with respect to contemporary methodological
debates in economics. This opens up a central issue for epistemology
and methodology that runs right through Weber’s ‘Wissenschaftslehre’,
an issue to which the greater part of his material investigations present a response, or at least attempt such a response. This can only be
very roughly outlined here, but two lines of conflict have to be here

problem of economic ‘developmental stages’, or rather, only in passing

Quite correctly the distinction between forms of economy and forms of
economic policy is now drawn more exactly. The stages which Schönberg
introduced and which, since modified and associated with Schmoller:
domestic economy, village economy—added to which there is a further
‘stage’ of the landed and patrimonial ruler’s household economy—town
economy, territorial economy, national economy—all these were in his
terminology defined by the form of the group concerned with economic
regulation. But this does not mean that the form of economic regulation
on the part of groups of different scope itself differed.

Then Weber introduces some examples: the policy of the German
territorial state consisted to a great extent in the adoption of regulations used in town economies, and its own new measures were not
specifically distinct from the ‘mercantilistic’ policy of specific patrimonial (and already relatively rational) state groups.70
Weber disputes the accepted correspondence of economic stages
(oikos, city and state) with type of regulation and added:

the manner in which work (Leistung) was specified, differentiated and

point of support for an economic policy, moreover, that when the scope
of this policy changed then it too changed in a related way. Any comparison of the Occident with Asia, and the modern with the ancient

which gainful transactions are made is very strongly determined by this.

the optimal pre-conditions of formal rationality of the economy and their
relations to material ‘demands’, whatever their form.71

Closing Remarks
Max Weber divided his ‘Basic Sociological Categories of Economic
Action’ into forty-four paragraphs.95 Weber prefaces this chapter with
the comment that he is not here concerned with economic theory, but
only with the definition ‘of a few commonly-used concepts’ and the
establishment of certain very elementary sociological relationships
with the economy.96 Weber had already characterised in his essay on
‘Objectivity’ such classificatory concepts as a ‘conceptual shorthand’
made necessary by the discursive nature of our knowledge97 but
which was unavoidable for the unambiguous representation of reality
within cultural analysis.
‘Specialisation and casuistry’ of types and categories is quite obviously sustained for the greater part by the empirical, by the history of
the economy. Historical analysis and presentation can however dispense with the profusion of such ‘specialisation and casuistry’, unlike
for instance a ‘rigorously economic theory of urban forms’, as Weber
remarked in respect of the economic concept and economic categories
of the city.98 The real subject-matter—the dynamic of reciprocallyrelated developments of economy and social (political, religious and
so forth) orders—is ‘for the time being’99 excluded from this categorical casuistry. Not, however, as consistently as Winckelmann suggests.100 For the categories derived from historical experience are even
in their formal definition materially related by Weber to this dynamic:

check.summary: The memo is exceptionally faithful to the four texts, accurately synthesizing Bruhns's arguments on Weber's comparative economic history, methodology, and critique of developmental stages. Minor verdict adjustments arise only from strict attribution requirements where statements cite multiple sources and one cited text omits a specific term (e.g., specific terms like 'Haushalten and Erwerben' or 'homo politicus/oeconomicus' not appearing across all co-cited texts).

items.statement: Read together, the works establish that Weber’s basic concepts arose within a continuous program of comparative economic history: explaining why rational enterprise capitalism based on formally free labour emerged in the Occident while other genuine forms of capitalism did not develop toward it [S1] [S2] [S4].
items.evidence: [S1] [PDF p. 1] 'Weber’s investigations in ancient economy, the medieval city, and the political, economic, social, and religious systems of China and India are for a great part an inventory of differences versus the occidental development of modern market-oriented capitalism based on the exploitation of (formally) free labor.' [S2] [PDF p. 1] 'Max Weber’s historical studies on economic forms and institutions should not be treated separately from his comprehensive interest in the connection between economy and society and forms of economy and rule.' [S4] [p. 39] 'economic history presents only a foundation, without which however productive study of any of the great realms of culture is inconceivable.'

items.statement: Ideal types distinguish historically specific configurations without turning them into stages, while the analysis moves across economic conduct, political organization, law, urban associations, religion, and coercion [S1] [S2] [S3] [S4].

items.statement: Capitalist forms depend on political organization, legal guarantees, associations, regulation, and access to coercive opportunities. items.statement: The autonomous northern inland city—with city law, autocephaly, taxation, market regulation, and bourgeois association—redirected conduct toward rational acquisition. It was indispensable or critical, but neither the sole cause nor simply identical with the southern commercial city conventionally treated as capitalism’s birthplace [S2] [S4].

(5) market regulation' [S4] [p. 64] 'The development of the medieval city was [for modern capitalism and the modern state] certainly not the sole crucial preliminary stage, and most certainly not its foundation, but it was a critical factor'

items.statement: The Chinese comparison shows that population growth, trade, money, and precious-metal inflows do not by themselves generate rational enterprise capitalism. Their effects depend on political structure, urban autonomy, bourgeois association, law, and economic ethos [S1] [S2].

In China, the absence of urban associations as bearers of the law'

items.statement: Religion contributes to the rationalization of conduct but does not independently create capitalism. The sources reject idealist or monocausal versions of the Weber thesis and embed economic ethos within a bundle of economic, legal, political, social, and technological conditions [S1] [S2] [S4].
items.evidence: [S1] [PDF p. 13] 'stand a whole bundle of factors, among which the religious is essential but only one of many: the factor that has contributed to the rationalization of the conduct of life' [S2] [PDF p. 4, 17] 'Weber had only pursued “one side of the causal relationship”... we shall not defend here two foolish and doctrinaire theses... that capitalism as an economic system was a creation of the Reformation' [S4] [p. 44] 'The univocal “idealist” explanation that renders capitalism the incarnation of a particular mentality... was of course an entirely mistaken interpretation'

items.statement: S3 extends the methodological critique to Polanyian and later historiography: neither ‘embedded’ nor ‘disembedded’ economy is sufficiently operative when detached from analysis of systems, conduct, extortion, and institutions. Classical categories must be tested against recent historical, archaeological, and anthropological research [S3].
items.evidence: [S3] [PDF p. 3, 5, 8] 'toute la dimension de l’extorsion dans les relations « économiques »... Mais le concept d’économie désencastrée, appliqué à Athènes, est-il vraiment moins nébuleux et plus opérationnel que celui d’économie encastrée ? En fin de compte, ne faudrait-il pas combiner autrement la relecture de nos classiques avec les recherches récentes (archéologiques, historiques et anthropologiques)'

items.statement: S4 reconstructs Weber’s break with universal genetic sequences by treating stages as analytical constructions whose elements can combine differently in concrete histories. S3 uses this point to reject Nafissi’s placement of Weber among primitivists and his assignment of antiquity to the oikos stage. S2 then applies the correction systematically to antiquity, the medieval city, and China [S2] [S3] [S4].
items.evidence: [S4] [p. 57] 'In the process of concrete historical development individual elements drawn from conceptually differentiated “stages” often combined into one distinct, specifically-formed concrete whole.' [S3] [PDF p. 6] 'expliquant que les Wirtschaftsstufen devaient être comprises comme des Idealtypen... Affirmer donc, comme le fait Nafissi... que, pour Weber, l’Antiquité se situe au niveau du stade économique de l’oikos... est tout simplement un malentendu.' [S2] [PDF p. 8-9, 13-14] 'detached the term from Rodbertus’ theory of development and used it... as an ideal-type model'

items.statement: S3 insists that the same distinctions between Haushalten and Erwerben apply to ancient and modern systems. S1 and S2 sharpen this into a distinction between politically oriented ancient capitalism and modern rational enterprise capitalism, preserving capitalism’s universality while specifying its divergent forms [S1] [S2] [S3].
items.evidence: [S3] [PDF p. 3-4] 'Car, pour Weber, la même logique d’analyse s’applique aux sociétés anciennes et modernes... Haushalten et Erwerben.' [S1] [PDF p. 9, 12] 'Weber considered ancient capitalism essentially to be a politically oriented capitalism... market-oriented capitalism' [S2] [PDF p. 8, 14] 'ancient capitalism does not proceed with a tendency towards convergence, but on the contrary with a tendency towards distance from the structural features of modern capitalism'

items.statement: S4 shows that Weber’s basic categories were generated through economic-historical research rather than imposed after an empirical phase. S2 clarifies their operation: ideal types order and weight historical material for a question and help form hypotheses, but do not themselves constitute substantive historical explanations [S2] [S4].
items.evidence: [S4] [p. 40, 64-65] 'The formerly well-established idea... that Weber’s work can be divided into two periods... stands revealed from this perspective as totally inappropriate... developed in the course of substantive investigations' [S2] [PDF p. 6] 'ordered and weighted in the light of a particular research question... is not a “hypothesis”, but seeks to guide the formation of hypotheses.'

items.statement: S4 identifies the medieval city as critical but not the sole foundation of modern capitalism. S2 narrows the claim by distinguishing the northern inland city from the southern commercial city and specifying autonomy, law, association, taxation, and regulation as the relevant mechanisms [S2] [S4].
items.evidence: [S4] [p. 64] 'The development of the medieval city was [for modern capitalism and the modern state] certainly not the sole crucial preliminary stage, and most certainly not its foundation, but it was a critical factor' [S2] [PDF p. 10-12] 'not the southern European commercial city... but the industrial inland city north of the Alps... (1) political autonomy, (2) autonomous legal statutes... (3) autocephaly, (4) tax power... (5) market regulation'

items.statement: S1 presents China as possessing several commonly proposed economic preconditions while lacking middle-class industrial capitalism. S2 specifies the missing configuration as city law, communal autonomy, a city bourgeoisie, urban economic policy, and calculable legal guarantees [S1] [S2].
items.evidence: [S1] [PDF p. 10] 'Why, asks Weber, “did not modern capitalism originate in China? It had several millennia to do so!”... China had no middle-class industrial capitalism' [S2] [PDF p. 14, 15] 'not a “polis” in the ancient sense – it had no city law – it did not know a city bourgeoisie... no city freedom – it did not form a community... could not carry out a “city economic policy”'

items.statement: S4 rejects the interpretation of Weber as making capitalism an expression of Protestant mentality. S1 and S2 incorporate religious ethics into the rationalization of conduct while subordinating monocausal claims to comparative analysis of political, legal, economic, technological, and social conditions [S1] [S2] [S4].

items.statement: S3 reports that reciprocity and redistribution may coexist, that redistribution can conceal extortion, and that embeddedness/disembeddedness remains conceptually unclear. It redirects analysis from isolated mechanisms or binaries toward historically specified systems combining conduct, institutions, and multiple modes of allocation [S3].
items.evidence: [S3] [PDF p. 3, 5, 8] 'un système dans lequel les deux formes d’économie coexistaient et interagissaient... toute la dimension de l’extorsion... items.statement: Bruhns rejects fundamental alterity: the same analytical distinctions, especially Haushalten and Erwerben, must be applied within every economic system [S3].
items.evidence: [S3] [PDF p. 3-4] 'Car, pour Weber, la même logique d’analyse s’applique aux sociétés anciennes et modernes, et il s’agit de déterminer, dans chaque système économique particulier... Haushalten et Erwerben.'

check.summary: The memo is broadly faithful to the four Bruhns texts on Weber's comparative economic history, correctly tracking the core themes of ideal types vs. stage theory, ancient vs. modern capitalism, the medieval city, China, and religion as one factor among many. However, it contains several misattributions and unsupported specifics, most notably wrongly attributing 'Rodbertus's followers' and Bücher-linked stage theory criticism to S4 in one place, misstating that S3 or others directly report Weber praising Bücher as an ideal-typical (S2 actually reports Weber defending Bücher's earlier stages as ideal types, but the 'How the ideas moved' item 1 wrongly implies S4 anticipates S3's specific critique of Nafissi, which is chronologically and substantively backwards since S3 (2008) predates and is independent of S4's (2006) argument, though thematically related this is the memo's own synthetic sequencing not asserted by the sources). Several 'Next steps' and 'Reading' items compress source content reasonably but sometimes attribute to a source a recommendation phrased more generally than the source states. The 'Beyond embeddedness' theme and Bruhns's critique of Nafissi's 'quasi social-democratic' reading are accurately supported by S3.

items.statement: Reading: Revisit the Bücher–Meyer controversy to distinguish ideal-typical economic forms from chronological stage theory [S1] [S2] [S3] [S4]
items.evidence: S1: 'occasioned by a heated dispute, started in the 1890s, between the ancient historian Eduard Meyer and the economist Karl Bücher... over the nature of the ancient economy.'
items.note: S1 mentions the Meyer-Bücher dispute only briefly in a footnote-like historical aside, not as a a live methodological recommendation; the claim holds better for S2, S3, S4 which discuss it substantively.

misreadings: The memo's 'How the ideas moved' item 1 implies a directional/derivative relationship between S4 (2006) and S3 (2008) regarding the critique of Nafissi and stage theory that is not established by the texts themselves; S3 develops its critique of Nafissi independently through close reading of Agrarverhältnisse, not via S4's argument.

The memo frames several of Bruhns's descriptive/analytical statements about what Weber's method accomplished (in S2's 'attempt at a balance sheet') as forward-looking prescriptive 'next steps', which subtly shifts the sources' historical-analytical register into a programmatic one.
missing: S1's extended discussion of Weber's contemporary political engagement (Naumann, agrarian capitalism in East Germany, the stock exchange commission, Weber's own definitions of capitalism across 1919-1920 texts) is largely omitted from the memo, though it is a substantial portion of S1.

S4's detailed account of the Jaffé-Sombart-Weber conflict over economic theory and the 'Declaration' defending 'rational construction of concepts, typologies and systems' is not reflected in the memo despite being central to S4's argument about history/theory relations.

S3's extensive review of the Polanyi volume (with Bresson, Testart, Renger, Maucourant, Servet, etc. and their debates on reciprocity/redistribution/extortion) is compressed drastically; specific named contributors and their distinct positions (e.g., Testart's rejection of redistribution, Bresson's critique of embeddedness) are underrepresented relative to their weight in the source.

The memo does not mention Bruhns's specific critique that Nafissi's 'quasi social-democratic' and 'better laissez-fairists' readings of Athens amount to a 'liberal and social-democrat' anachronistic projection—an important critical point in S3.

check.summary: The memo is broadly faithful to the four Bruhns texts on Weber's comparative economic history, and most core claims about ideal types, ancient vs. modern capitalism, the medieval city, China, and religion are supported across S1/S2/S3/S4. The clearest slip is a directly diagnostic one: statement 22 repeats the exact 'Bücher, Rodbertus's followers... [S2][S4]' error the instructions warn against—only S2 names Rodbertus. A few other citations attribute content to S4 that actually appears in S2 (e.g., the anti-Reformation-determinism claim), and several 'still open'/'next steps' items are the memo's own reasonable extrapolations rather than statements the sources pose explicitly as open questions. S3's role in the broad omnibus lists (e.g., item 1's 'religion, urban associations' or item 50's Weber–Sombart comparison) is thin, since S3 barely touches those specific topics.

Statement 17 attributes to S4 a rejection of the 'Protestant mentality' interpretation of capitalism that is more precisely sourced to S1's/S2's shared footnote quoting Weber's 'Antikritisches' rebuttal, not explicit content in S4 itself.
missing: S1's extensive discussion of Weber's direct political and institutional engagement (Bourse Commission, agrarian capitalism in the German East, the Grundriss der Sozialökonomik's structure and Weber's own reserved topics) is largely absent from the memo despite being a major portion of S1.

S2's detailed account of the Bücher-Weber editorial conflict over the Grundriss (Weber's anger at Bücher's 'meagre' contribution, and how this catalyzed Weber's own systematic sociology) is not reflected in the memo.

S3's substantial review of the edited Polanyi colloquium volume (with contributions by Maucourant, Renger, Testart, Servet, Bresson, Lafont, Michel, Rede, Sauvage, Jursa, Graslin-Thomé, Vivel, Perlès, Scheid-Tissinier, Parise, Descat, Pébarthe, Becquelin, Chapman) is reduced to a single generic reading recommendation, omitting its rich diversity of positions.

S4's extensive discussion of the reception history of Weber within the discipline of economic history (Braudel, Rostovtzeff, Finley, Heuss, Engerman, Norkus, Kaufhold) is entirely omitted from the memo's account of 'how the ideas moved'.

check.summary: The memo is exceptionally faithful to the four source articles by Hinnerk Bruhns, accurately synthesising Bruhns's reconstruction of Max Weber's comparative economic history, methodology of ideal types, and substantive analyses of antiquity, the medieval city, and China. A small number of multi-source citations are marked partly supported because one of the cited sources does not explicitly mention a specific name or concept (e.g., Bücher/Meyer controversy in S1, or specific China/religion details across S4).

items.statement: Read together, the works establish that Weber’s basic concepts arose within a continuous program of comparative economic history: explaining why rational enterprise capitalism based on formally free labour emerged in the Occident while other genuine forms of capitalism did not develop toward it [S1] [S2] [S4]. Ideal types distinguish historically specific configurations without turning them into stages, while the analysis moves across economic conduct, political organization, law, urban associations, religion, and coercion [S1] [S2] [S3] [S4].
items.evidence: [S1 p. 1] 'Weber’s investigations in ancient economy, the medieval city, and the political, economic, social, and religious systems of China and India are for a great part an inventory of differences versus the occidental development of modern market-oriented capitalism based on the exploitation of (formally) free labor.' [S2 p. 1] 'His analyses of the modern economy in general, and specifically of modern bourgeois enterprise capitalism with its organization of (formally) free labour, are largely based on comparative studies of economic forms and institutions in societies far removed in time and space.' [S4 p. 41] 'If we survey the entire period of Weber’s writing, we can certainly detect a process of development in respect of economic history... The Protestant Ethic... Agrarian Relationships in Antiquity... The City... The Economic Ethic of World Religions'. [S3 p. 3-4] 'Car, pour Weber, la même logique d’analyse s’applique aux sociétés anciennes et modernes... et d'Erwerben.'

items.statement: The historical specificity of modern capitalism: Capitalism is historically widespread, but modern capitalism is the distinctive configuration of rational, continuous enterprise, capital accounting, calculable law, markets, and formally free labour. The sources converge against equating all acquisitive activity with modern occidental capitalism [S1] [S2] [S4].
items.evidence: [S1 p. 6-7] 'a decisive criterion, the rational-capitalist organization of (formally) free labor as a business... Weber contrast this middle-class business capitalism with other forms of capitalism and capitalistic enterprises, which have existed in all the civilized countries in the world' [S2 p. 1] 'modern bourgeois enterprise capitalism with its organization of (formally) free labour, are largely based on comparative studies' [S4 p. 64] 'how did the capitalistic drive for valorisation come to create that particular form of ‘free’ labour that was unknown in Antiquity?'

items.statement: Ideal types against developmental stages: Ideal types select and weight historical elements for causal inquiry; they are neither empirical reality nor a sequence through which every society must pass. This position rejects linear readings of oikos, town, and national economy associated with stage theory and with misreadings of Bücher and Weber [S2] [S3] [S4].
items.evidence: [S2 p. 8-9] 'Weber did not use the stage theory as a model of successive economic forms over time, but as an ideal-type model with which empirical economic systems could be analysed. Thus, as he demonstrates with the example of antiquity, the Haushaltswirtschaft could appear at the end of a development, not necessarily at the beginning.' [S3 p. 6] 'expliquant que les Wirtschaftsstufen devaient être comprises comme des Idealtypen, ce que Bücher lui-même n’avait pas compris... Affirmer donc, comme le fait Nafissi... que, pour Weber, l’Antiquité se situe au niveau du stade économique de l’oikos... est tout simplement un malentendu.' [S4 p. 56-57] 'Weber defends Bücher’s system, conceiving his stages as ideal types, hence not in the sense of a determinate chronological sequence... Weber insists that the ancient oikos lay in fact at the end of a process of development, not at its beginning.'

items.statement: Economic history and theory are mutually constitutive: Against the opposition between fact collection and abstract theory, Weberian inquiry joins detailed historical investigation to rational concept, typology, and system construction. S4 establishes this as a continuous feature of Weber’s work, while S2 specifies that concepts order evidence and support hypothesis formation [S2] [S4].
items.evidence: [S2 p. 6] 'It was a matter of forming hypotheses from empirical, historical facts and of posing problems. According to Weber, an ideal type “is not a ‘hypothesis’, but seeks to guide the formation of hypotheses.' [S4 p. 51] '“We both attribute the greatest conceivable significance to so-called ‘theory’ in economics, by which we mean the rational construction of concepts, typologies and systems... “...to replace that alternative between ‘historical’ or ‘theoretical’ economics that has for too long dominated discussion' [S4 p. 40] 'stands revealed from this perspective as totally inappropriate.'

items.statement: Ancient capitalism without an immanent modernity: Ancient capitalism was capitalist in the economic sense but predominantly politically and militarily oriented. Slavery, war, constrained markets, limited calculation, unstable capital formation, and the precarious entrepreneur produced structural divergence rather than an incomplete version of modern capitalism [S1] [S2] [S4].
items.evidence: [S1 p. 9] 'limits on the transport capacity... economically determined liability in capital stock and capital formation... technical limitations of the exploitation of slave labor... politically and socially precarious position of the entrepreneur... Weber considered ancient capitalism essentially to be a politically oriented capitalism.' [S2 p. 8] 'limits on the transport capacity... lability in capital stock and capital formation as well as the technical limitations of the exploitation of slave labour... precarious position of the entrepreneur... Weber considered ancient capitalism essentially to be a politically oriented capitalism.' [S4 p. 63] 'the development of ancient economy and of ancient capitalism tend not to converge upon, but rather diverge from, the structural features of modern capitalism.'

items.statement: One analytical logic, different economic systems: S3 rejects the claim that ancient economies possess a fundamentally alien economic logic: Haushalten and Erwerben must be identified within each system. S1, S2, and S4 develop the corresponding comparative distinctions among politically oriented capitalism, enterprise capitalism, homo politicus, and homo oeconomicus [S1] [S2] [S3] [S4].
items.evidence: [S3 p. 3-4] 'La mise en cause de la doctrine de l’altérité fondamentale de l’économie antique est poursuivie par Alain Bresson... Car, pour Weber, la même logique d’analyse s’applique aux sociétés anciennes et modernes, et il s’agit de déterminer, dans chaque système économique particulier... Haushalten et Erwerben.' [S1 p. 9-12] 'purely economically oriented capitalism... politically oriented capitalism... market-oriented capitalism' [S2 p. 12] 'homo oeconomicus, whereas the polis of antiquity... The ancient citizen was homo politicus' [S4 p. 65] 'ideal-typical contrast between ‘homo politicus’ (the ancient city = associations of citizens and warriors whose economic action is primarily politically and militarily oriented) and ‘homo oeconomicus’ (medieval city—primarily economically-oriented).'

items.statement: Political and legal institutions shape economic orientation: Capitalist forms depend on political organization, legal guarantees, associations, regulation, and access to coercive opportunities. The state can provide calculability while also enabling politically guaranteed gain, bureaucratization, and particular capitalist interests [S1] [S2] [S4].
items.evidence: [S1 p. 13] 'It must be able to rely on the continuity, security and practicality of the functioning of the legal order, on the rational in principle predictable character of legal judgements and administration... bureaucratization... mobilization of the resources of the state for the enforcement of particular capitalist interests.' [S2 p. 11, 16] 'rational product of the imperial administration... legal foundations of a free, cooperatively regulated constitution of industry and commerce... patrimonial character of administration and law-making stood in the way of a rationally calculable functioning' [S4 p. 62] 'the existence, or non-existence, of corporate groups with material powers of economic regulation... The form in which gainful transactions are made is very strongly determined by this.'

items.statement: The medieval city as critical but insufficient: The autonomous northern inland city—with city law, autocephaly, taxation, market regulation, and bourgeois association—redirected conduct toward rational acquisition. It was indispensable or critical, but neither the sole cause nor simply identical with the southern commercial city conventionally treated as capitalism’s birthplace [S2] [S4].
items.evidence: [S2 p. 10-12] 'it was not the southern European commercial city, as was generally assumed, but the industrial inland city north of the Alps... (1) political autonomy, (2) autonomous legal statutes... (3) autocephaly, (4) tax power... (5) market regulation... nevertheless indispensable as a highly decisive factor in their emergence' [S4 p. 64] 'The development of the medieval city was [for modern capitalism and the modern state] certainly not the sole crucial preliminary stage, and most certainly not its foundation, but it was a critical factor in its development and cannot be disregarded.'

items.statement: Material preconditions do not explain capitalist emergence: The Chinese comparison shows that population growth, trade, money, and precious-metal inflows do not by themselves generate rational enterprise capitalism. Their effects depend on political structure, urban autonomy, bourgeois association, law, and economic ethos [S1] [S2].
items.evidence: [S1 p. 10] 'Why, asks Weber, “did not modern capitalism originate in China? It had several millennia to do so!”... In arguing in this way Weber was going against the normal interpretation of economic historians that the rise of capitalism was based on the large increase in population, the supply of precious metal, an enhanced money economy, intensive trade' [S2 p. 13] 'trade with Europe and the resulting increase in the influx of precious metals... did not bring about any capitalist phenomena... Nor had the colossal increase in the population provided any incentive... Strong population growth, circulation of precious metals and strengthening of the money economy, were factors that in economic history at the time of Weber were seen as decisive'

items.statement: Religion as one condition among many: Religion contributes to the rationalization of conduct but does not independently create capitalism. The sources reject idealist or monocausal versions of the Weber thesis and embed economic ethos within a bundle of economic, legal, political, social, and technological conditions [S1] [S2] [S4].
items.evidence: [S1 p. 13-14] 'stands a whole bundle of factors, among which the religious is essential but only one of many: the factor that has contributed to the rationalization of the conduct of life' [S2 p. 17 n. 4] '“we shall not defend here two foolish and doctrinaire theses in any form: (1) that the capitalist spirit […] could have originated only as an expression of certain influences of the Reformation, and (2) that capitalism as an economic system was a creation of the Reformation”' [S4 p. 44] '“The univocal ‘idealist’ explanation that renders capitalism the incarnation of a particular mentality... is a way of avoiding the thought of Marx.” That was of course an entirely mistaken interpretation, both in respect of Weber and for Marx.'

items.statement: Beyond embeddedness and the primitivist-modernist binary: S3 extends the methodological critique to Polanyian and later historiography: neither ‘embedded’ nor ‘disembedded’ economy is sufficiently operative when detached from analysis of systems, conduct, extortion, and institutions. Classical categories must be tested against recent historical, archaeological, and anthropological research [S3].
items.evidence: [S3 p. 3, 8] 'Et ce concept, trop marqué au goût de Testart par l’idée de don et contre-don, néglige selon lui toute la dimension de l’extorsion...
