En fin de compte, ne faudrait-il pas combiner autrement la relecture de nos classiques avec les recherches récentes (archéologiques, historiques et anthropologiques) sur le marché... ?'

items.statement: From economic stages to ideal-typical combinations: S4 reconstructs Weber’s break with universal genetic sequences by treating stages as analytical constructions whose elements can combine differently in concrete histories. S3 uses this point to reject Nafissi’s placement of Weber among primitivists and his assignment of antiquity to the oikos stage. S2 then applies the correction systematically to antiquity, the medieval city, and China [S2] [S3] [S4].
items.evidence: [S4 p. 57] 'In the process of concrete historical development individual elements drawn from conceptually differentiated ‘stages’ often combined into one distinct, specifically-formed concrete whole.' [S3 p. 6] 'Affirmer donc, comme le fait Nafissi... que, pour Weber, l’Antiquité se situe au niveau du stade économique de l’oikos et compter Weber... dans le bataillon des primitivistes est tout simplement un malentendu.' [S2 p. 8-14] 'Weber did not use the stage theory as a model of successive economic forms over time, but as an ideal-type model with which empirical economic systems could be analysed... ancient economy, the medieval city and China'

items.statement: From ancient-modern opposition to differentiated capitalism: S3 insists that the same distinctions between Haushalten and Erwerben apply to ancient and modern systems. S1 and S2 sharpen this into a distinction between politically oriented ancient capitalism and modern rational enterprise capitalism, preserving capitalism’s universality while specifying its divergent forms [S1] [S2] [S3].
items.evidence: [S3 p. 3-4] 'Car, pour Weber, la même logique d’analyse s’applique aux sociétés anciennes et modernes... Haushalten et Erwerben.' [S1 p. 9-10] 'Weber considered ancient capitalism essentially to be a politically oriented capitalism... modern economically oriented capitalism' [S2 p. 8, 12] 'ancient capitalism essentially to be a politically oriented capitalism... modern enterprise capitalism'

items.statement: From economic history to sociological basic concepts: S4 shows that Weber’s basic categories were generated through economic-historical research rather than imposed after an empirical phase. S2 clarifies their operation: ideal types order and weight historical material for a question and help form hypotheses, but do not themselves constitute substantive historical explanations [S2] [S4].
items.evidence: [S4 p. 64-65] 'quite plainly it was developed in the course of substantive investigations so that order could be introduced into the ‘unconnected variety of Fakta’; it would have been extraordinary if it had happened the other way around.' [S2 p. 6] 'historical material, the historical and empirical facts, was ordered and weighted in the light of a particular research question... An ideal type “is not a ‘hypothesis’, but seeks to guide the formation of hypotheses.'

items.statement: From the city as birthplace to the city as institutional configuration: S4 identifies the medieval city as critical but not the sole foundation of modern capitalism. S2 narrows the claim by distinguishing the northern inland city from the southern commercial city and specifying autonomy, law, association, taxation, and regulation as the relevant mechanisms [S2] [S4].
items.evidence: [S4 p. 64] 'The development of the medieval city was [for modern capitalism and the modern state] certainly not the sole crucial preliminary stage, and most certainly not its foundation, but it was a critical factor in its development and cannot be disregarded.' (3) autocephaly, (4) tax power... (5) market regulation'

items.statement: From material endowments to institutional sufficiency: S1 presents China as possessing several commonly proposed economic preconditions while lacking middle-class industrial capitalism. S2 specifies the missing configuration as city law, communal autonomy, a city bourgeoisie, urban economic policy, and calculable legal guarantees [S1] [S2].
items.evidence: [S1 p. 10] 'normal interpretation of economic historians that the rise of capitalism was based on the large increase in population, the supply of precious metal, an enhanced money economy, intensive trade... China had no middle-class industrial capitalism' [S2 p. 14-16] 'no city law – it did not know a city bourgeoisie... no city freedom – it did not form a community... could not carry out a “city economic policy”... rationally calculable functioning of administration and administration of justice'

items.statement: From religious causation to a bundle of conditions: S4 rejects the interpretation of Weber as making capitalism an expression of Protestant mentality. S1 and S2 incorporate religious ethics into the rationalization of conduct while subordinating monocausal claims to comparative analysis of political, legal, economic, technological, and social conditions [S1] [S2] [S4].
items.evidence: [S4 p. 44] '“The univocal ‘idealist’ explanation that renders capitalism the incarnation of a particular mentality... is a way of avoiding the thought of Marx.” That was of course an entirely mistaken interpretation' [S1 p. 13-14] 'stand a whole bundle of factors, among which the religious is essential but only one of many: the factor that has contributed to the rationalization of the conduct of life' [S2 p. 3-4, 17 n. 4] 'Weber had only pursued “one side of the causal relationship”... “we shall not defend here two foolish and doctrinaire theses in any form: (1) that the capitalist spirit […] could have originated only as an expression of certain influences of the Reformation”'

items.statement: From Polanyian modes to analysis of economic systems: S3 reports that reciprocity and redistribution may coexist, that redistribution can conceal extortion, and that embeddedness/disembeddedness remains conceptually unclear. It redirects analysis from isolated mechanisms or binaries toward historically specified systems combining conduct, institutions, and multiple modes of allocation [S3].
items.evidence: [S3 p. 3, 5, 8] 'un système dans lequel les deux formes d’économie coexistaient et interagissaient...
